name: Candid photo method

card.summary: Choosing or staging natural-looking, in-the-moment photos for dating profiles so a person looks relaxed and approachable rather than posed.
card.note: Specific research on candid versus posed photos is limited; guidance is mostly anecdotal.

quick.overview:
The candid photo method is the practice of using natural, caught-in-the-moment photos on dating profiles in place of stiff posed shots. The payoff described by practitioners is that a person looks more relaxed and approachable, and that a varied set of pictures shows different sides of them.

Research on dating-app photos is limited to broad findings, such as a 2016 Tinder study in which male profiles with three pictures drew many more matches than profiles with none. Advice about candid photos specifically comes mostly from forum users and friends giving feedback.
quick.how: People typically ask a friend to take photos during activities, choose shots showing different settings, expressions and sides of themselves, and avoid sets of near-identical posed pictures. Some combine it with grooming and clothing choices before the photos are taken.
quick.risks: There is no physical risk. Photos must be of the person themselves, and misrepresenting appearance through heavy editing can disappoint on meeting in person.

lead: The candid photo method is a profile-photo approach used in online dating communities: instead of a set of posed or repetitive portraits, a person uses natural-looking images captured during real activities, with varied settings and expressions.[1] It is applied to apps such as Tinder, and in looksmaxxing circles it belongs with style and presentation tips that change how a face and body come across without altering them.

In one T Nation thread about getting a girlfriend, a commenter criticized a profile whose pictures were all essentially the same posed shot and said a good set shows different sides of the person.[1] That feedback captures the core of the method: variety and naturalness over a single polished pose.

Published research on dating profiles is broader. A 2016 study by Gareth Tyson and colleagues using test accounts found male profiles with three pictures received far more matches than profiles with none, and an OkCupid analysis by co-founder Christian Rudder found the most attractive men, as rated by women on the site, received about eleven times as many messages as the least attractive.[2]

chain: Take natural photos in real settings
Looks more approachable and authentic to viewers
angle.text: Practitioners use candid photos so a profile shows a person relaxed and in context, rather than posed and repetitive. They rely on friends taking shots during everyday activities and select a set that shows different sides.

paras: Candid profile photos are images taken without obvious posing, such as during travel, hobbies or social events. Commenters in online discussions contrast them with sets of identical posed portraits, which one described as off-putting, arguing that a profile should show different sides of a person.[1]

Dating-app research has examined photo count and attractiveness rather than candid style specifically. The 2016 Tinder experiment used test accounts and found that men with three photos got many more matches than men with none; its authors used only people of average attractiveness, so it did not test how attractiveness changed results.[2] OkCupid data reported by Rudder found that men rated most attractive received far more messages than those rated least attractive.[2]
